title: Writing an AI Product Strategy and One-Page Vision
summary: Learn to write a defensible AI product strategy and a one-page vision document that aligns stakeholders, clarifies positioning and differentiation, and connects AI capabilities to real customer and business value.
objectives: Articulate a clear AI product vision narrative that motivates teams and stakeholders
Define positioning and differentiation grounded in defensible AI advantages (data, workflow, distribution)
Translate strategy into measurable outcomes and a prioritized set of bets
Distinguish genuine AI moats from commodity capabilities and feature parity
Produce a one-page vision document that fits on a single page and survives executive review

quiz.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a durable moat for an AI product?
options: Access to a general-purpose LLM API
quiz.why: General API access, prompts, and chat UIs are easily replicated commodities. A proprietary data flywheel compounds with usage and is hard for competitors to copy.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the "What we are NOT doing" section in a one-page vision?
options: To pad the document to a full page
To impose the discipline of saying no and sharpen strategic choices
To document technical limitations of the model
quiz.why: Explicit non-goals force real trade-offs, which is what separates a focused strategy from a wish list of features.

quiz.q: Which question best pressure-tests an AI product's defensibility?
options: Does the model use the latest architecture?
If a competitor had the same model API tomorrow, what would they still lack?
How many parameters does the model have?
Is the UI better than competitors'?
quiz.why: This question isolates what is truly hard to copy — data, workflow, distribution, domain depth — versus commodity model access.

quiz.q: In the Today–Tension–Future–Bridge narrative structure, what does the 'Bridge' represent?
options: The capability that makes the future state possible
quiz.why: The Bridge is the enabling capability that connects the painful Today to the aspirational Future the product creates.

quiz.q: Name one AI-specific guardrail metric (beyond a growth north-star) that an AI product strategy should track.
quiz.answer: Quality/accuracy, trust and safety, cost-per-inference, or latency
quiz.why: AI strategies must guard against degrading quality, safety, or unit economics; any of these guardrails prevents optimizing growth at the expense of the product's integrity.

quiz.q: Why is a strong 'why now' statement especially important for AI products?
quiz.answer: It names the specific enabling shift (cheaper inference, new model capabilities, data availability, regulation) that makes the timing credible
quiz.why: AI timing depends on recent enabling shifts; naming them makes the opportunity believable rather than speculative hype.

body_markdown:
## Why AI Product Strategy Is Different

AI products carry uncertainty that traditional software does not: model behavior is probabilistic, data is a first-class asset, and capabilities can be rapidly commoditized by foundation-model providers. A strong AI product strategy answers a deceptively simple question: **why will this product win, and why will it keep winning?** It cannot rest on "we use AI" — that is table stakes. It must rest on a defensible advantage and a clear connection to customer value.

Strategy is a set of choices about where to play and how to win. The one-page vision is the artifact that communicates those choices crisply enough that any stakeholder — an engineer, an executive, a sales rep — can repeat it.

## The Core Components of an AI Product Strategy

1. **Customer and problem** — Who hurts, how badly, and how often? AI is expensive and uncertain, so the problem must justify it. Prefer problems where current solutions are slow, costly, or impossible without intelligence.
2. **Vision narrative** — A short story of the future state your product creates. It should be aspirational but believable.
3. **Positioning** — The category you compete in and the reference point in the customer's mind ("the X for Y").
4. **Differentiation and moat** — What makes you hard to copy. For AI this typically comes from proprietary or compounding data, deep workflow integration, distribution, or a system of models tuned to a specific domain — *not* the base model itself.
5. **Strategic bets** — The 3-5 things you are betting on, and the assumptions behind each.
6. **Outcomes and metrics** — How you will measure progress (north-star metric plus guardrails like quality, cost-per-inference, and trust/safety metrics).

## Defensibility: Real Moats vs. Commodity Capabilities

Ask: if a competitor had the same model API tomorrow, what would they still lack? Durable AI advantages include:

- **Data flywheel** — usage generates proprietary data that improves the product, which attracts more usage.
- **Workflow lock-in** — the product is embedded in how work gets done, with switching costs.
- **Distribution** — existing channels, integrations, or an installed base.
- **Domain depth** — evaluation sets, fine-tuning, guardrails, and tacit knowledge competitors lack.

Commodity (not moats by themselves): access to a general LLM, a clever prompt, a chat UI, generic embeddings. These are easily replicated.

## Writing the Vision Narrative

Good vision narratives are concrete and customer-anchored. Use the structure: **Today** (the painful status quo), **Tension** (why it persists / why now), **Future** (the world your product enables), **Bridge** (the capability that makes it possible). Keep it to a paragraph or two. Avoid hype words; describe observable outcomes ("a claims adjuster resolves a case in minutes, not days").

"Why now?" is critical for AI — name the specific enabling shift (cheaper inference, multimodal models, regulatory change, data availability) so the timing is credible.

## The One-Page Vision Template

Fit all of this on a single page:

- **Vision statement** (1-2 sentences)
- **Target customer & problem** (who, pain, frequency)
- **Why now** (the enabling shift)
- **How we win** (positioning + differentiation/moat)
- **Strategic bets** (3-5 bullets with key assumption each)
- **Success metrics** (north star + 2-3 guardrails including a quality/trust metric)
- **What we are NOT doing** (explicit non-goals)

The non-goals section is what separates strategy from a wish list. Saying no is the discipline that makes the document defensible.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Tech-first framing** — leading with the model instead of the customer outcome.
- **No defensibility** — a vision any competitor with an API key could execute.
- **Vague metrics** — "improve engagement" without a target or guardrail.
- **Ignoring trust and risk** — AI strategies must address quality, safety, and failure modes as part of the value proposition.
- **Too long** — if it doesn't fit on one page, the choices aren't sharp enough.

## Putting It Together

Draft the narrative first to get conviction, then compress into the one-pager, then pressure-test defensibility with the "same API tomorrow" question. Socialize it, capture objections, and iterate. The one-pager becomes the anchor for your roadmap — every initiative should trace back to a strategic bet on the page.

slides.title: Writing an AI Product Strategy and One-Page Vision
slides.sub: Positioning, differentiation, and a crisp vision narrative
slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll learn how to write a defensible AI product strategy and compress it into a one-page vision that aligns every stakeholder. By the end, you'll be able to articulate why your AI product will win and keep winning.

slides.title: Why AI Strategy Is Different
bullets: Model behavior is probabilistic, not deterministic
Data is a first-class strategic asset
Capabilities are quickly commoditized by foundation models
"We use AI" is table stakes, not a strategy
slides.narration: AI products carry uncertainty traditional software doesn't. Models are probabilistic, data is a core asset, and base capabilities get commoditized fast as foundation-model providers improve. So your strategy can't rest on simply using AI. It must answer why you'll win and keep winning, grounded in something hard to copy.

slides.title: Core Components of the Strategy
bullets: Customer and problem worth the cost of AI
Vision narrative — the believable future state
Positioning — the category and reference point
slides.narration: A complete AI strategy has six parts: the customer and a problem painful enough to justify AI, a vision narrative, positioning in a category, your differentiation or moat, the three to five bets you're making, and the metrics that prove progress. Each section forces a real choice.

slides.title: Real Moats vs. Commodity
bullets: Test: same model API tomorrow — what do they still lack?
Moats: data flywheel, workflow lock-in, distribution, domain depth
Commodity: generic LLM access, clever prompts, chat UI
Defensibility compounds with usage over time
slides.narration: Pressure-test defensibility with a simple question: if a competitor had your exact model API tomorrow, what would they still lack? Durable advantages come from a data flywheel, deep workflow integration, distribution, and domain depth. A general model, a prompt, or a chat interface alone is commodity — easily replicated.

slides.title: The Data Flywheel
bullets: Compounds into a widening, hard-to-copy lead
slides.narration: The strongest AI moat is often a data flywheel. Usage generates proprietary data that no one else has, that data improves your models and product, and the better product attracts more usage. Over time this compounds into a lead competitors can't shortcut, because they can't buy your accumulated, domain-specific data.

slides.title: Writing the Vision Narrative
bullets: Name a credible "why now" enabling shift
slides.narration: Write the narrative using four beats: Today, the painful status quo; Tension, why it persists and why now; Future, the world your product enables; and Bridge, the capability that makes it possible. Anchor it in observable outcomes — like resolving a claim in minutes not days — and name the specific shift that makes the timing right.

slides.title: The One-Page Vision Template
bullets: Target customer, problem, and why now
slides.code:
# One-Page Vision
Vision: ...
Customer & Problem: ...
Why Now: ...
How We Win: ...
Bets: 1) ... 2) ... 3) ...
Metrics: north-star + guardrails
NOT doing: ...
slides.narration: Everything fits on one page: a one or two sentence vision, the target customer and why now, how you win, three to five strategic bets each with its key assumption, success metrics including a quality or trust guardrail, and crucially, what you are NOT doing. The non-goals section is what turns a wish list into a strategy.

slides.title: Metrics That Matter for AI
slides.narration: AI strategies need a north-star metric tied to value, plus guardrails unique to AI: a quality metric like resolution rate, trust and safety measures, and operational guardrails like cost-per-inference and latency. These prevent you from optimizing growth while quality or unit economics quietly collapse.

slides.title: Pitfalls and Next Steps
bullets: No defensibility — anyone with an API could do it
Vague metrics; ignoring trust and risk
slides.narration: Avoid leading with the model, having no real moat, vague metrics, and ignoring risk. The workflow: draft the narrative to build conviction, compress it to one page, pressure-test defensibility, then socialize and iterate. The one-pager becomes the anchor for your roadmap — every initiative should trace back to a bet on the page.
